answer.label: Not Wayne Dyer — an older saying he reprinted without credit
answer.authorDates: Earliest documented user, 1927 · Flatbush Congregational Church, Brooklyn
answer.sourceLine: Wayne Dyer did print this line — but in his 1980 book ‘The Sky’s the Limit,’ he offered it “without attribution,” as an already-circulating saying he never claimed to coin. Quote Investigator traces the earliest known instance to a 1927 sermon by the Reverend Clarence H. Wilson, reported in the ‘Brooklyn Daily Eagle’ — and even that origin is held tentatively.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Sermon by Rev. Clarence H. Wilson, reported in the ‘Brooklyn Daily Eagle’

source.excerpt: How old would you be if you didn’t know how old you are?
trail: The earliest known instance is a 1927 sermon by Reverend Clarence H. Wilson, reported in the ‘Brooklyn Daily Eagle,’ per Quote Investigator, which “tentatively considers Wilson to be the originator.”

Actress Ruth Gordon credited the line to baseball legend Satchel Paige in 1977 testimony before the U.S. House Select Committee on Aging, and her husband, director Garson Kanin, repeated the Paige attribution in his 1978 book ‘It Takes a Long Time To Become Young.’
Wayne Dyer reprinted the saying in his 1980 book ‘The Sky’s the Limit’ but did so “without attribution,” presenting it as received wisdom rather than his own coinage.
source.excerptNote: The 1927 wording asked “how old you are”; the now-standard “how old you were” variant appears in Ruth Gordon’s 1977 congressional testimony crediting Satchel Paige.

source.rightsNote: The saying is documented in a 1927 ‘Brooklyn Daily Eagle’ report of a sermon — a pre-1931 U.S. publication, and therefore public domain — and the now-standard “how old you were” variant appears in Ruth Gordon’s 1977 testimony in the public U.S. congressional record. It is an old folk expression owned by no one, not original to Wayne Dyer.

author.heading: The 1927 preacher, not the 1980 self-help author
author.metaLine: fl. 1927 · Pastor, Flatbush Congregational Church, Brooklyn
author.bio: The Reverend Clarence H. Wilson is the earliest person documented asking “How old would you be if you didn’t know how old you are?” — in a 1927 sermon reported by the ‘Brooklyn Daily Eagle.’ Quote Investigator credits him only tentatively, noting a better citation could push the origin earlier. Either way, the line is a folk saying that circulated for decades before Wayne Dyer reprinted it.

misattribution.heading: How Wayne Dyer — and Satchel Paige — got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a genuine old saying that has been pinned on several famous names. Wayne Dyer is one of the more recent hosts, but the record shows he passed the line along rather than originated it.

items.why: Dyer printed the expression in his 1980 book ‘The Sky’s the Limit,’ but did so “without attribution,” treating it as established wisdom. That later got flattened into “Wayne Dyer said it.”

Actress Ruth Gordon attributed the line to Paige in 1977 congressional testimony, and her husband Garson Kanin repeated it in a 1978 book — roughly half a century after the earliest known use. No contemporaneous source shows Paige coining it.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented instance is a 1927 sermon by Rev. Clarence H. Wilson, per Quote Investigator — and that attribution is itself held tentatively. It is an old folk saying, not a Wayne Dyer original.

context.heading: Why the mix-up sticks
lead: The line is a compact bit of aphorism — the kind of “age is a mindset” wisdom that attaches easily to whichever inspirational name a reader already trusts. Satchel Paige, who pitched in the majors into his forties, made an irresistible host; Wayne Dyer, a best-selling self-help author, made another.
Because the saying circulated anonymously for decades before either man used it, no single “correct” author exists to displace the myth — which is exactly why it keeps drifting from name to name.
context.pull: An old folk saying that keeps changing owners — are/were, Wilson/Paige/Dyer.
